title: Shravan Kumar
hookLine: a king dies at midnight, and a boy with no name in the oldest text becomes the picture of serving your parents
carry: honor mother and father as gods
tomorrow: what does a bad dream tell Bharata?
last: AMENDS BEGIN WITH TELLING THE TRUTH.

cards: In many Indian homes, children hear about the young man at the river long before anyone reads them the Ramayana.
In those tellings he has a name, Shravan Kumar, and a picture: a son carrying his blind parents on pilgrimage, one in each of two baskets hung from a pole across his shoulders.
Grandparents tell it at bedtime as the story of a good son. Here's the surprise. In Valmiki's Ramayana, the young man has no name, and there are no baskets.

teach.b: First, the night ends. Dasharatha finishes the story, and he knows what it means. He tells Kausalya his eyes are failing; he can't see her anymore.
If only Rama would come back and touch me now, he says. And somewhere past midnight, still speaking of his son, the old king dies. In the morning the attendants come to wake him and find him gone.
No son is there for the last rites: Rama is in the forest, and Bharata far away in his grandfather's kingdom.

teach.h: A BODY KEPT IN OIL FOR BHARATA.
teach.b: So the ministers lay the king's body in a vessel of oil, to keep it until Bharata comes, and send riders to Kekaya with strict orders: say nothing. Just bring him. Now the boy at the river.
Valmiki calls him simply the young ascetic, the hermit's son.

teach.h: LATER: SHRAVAN KUMAR, AND THE BASKETS.
teach.b: Later retellings call him Shravan Kumar and add the pilgrimage, his blind parents carried in two baskets on a pole.

teach.h: MATRU DEVO BHAVA. PITRU DEVO BHAVA.
teach.b: Why did a boy with no name become a children's story told across much of India? Because he carries a teaching Hindus hold close.

teach.h: HONOR MOTHER AND FATHER AS GODS.
teach.b: The Taittiriya Upanishad gives a student leaving his teacher these parting words: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you.
Caring for your parents, especially as they grow old, isn't only kindness in Hinduism. It's a sacred duty, close to worship.

That's why grandparents tell this story at bedtime, and why calling someone a Shravan Kumar is high praise. Even the name fits: shravana is connected with hearing, and this boy was killed by an archer who shot at a sound.

how: Shravan Kumar is a common children's story across much of India, told to teach care for parents, and his name is still used as praise for a devoted son or daughter.

games.q: a friend asks: if Valmiki's boy has no name, why does Shravan Kumar matter so much? what fits today's teaching?
o: he stands for caring for parents as a sacred duty, close to worship.
he matters because Valmiki tells his whole life story.

games.why: the name stands for a child who serves their parents. the Taittiriya Upanishad says: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you.

practice: Bring to mind someone older who looked after you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, or anyone who once carried something for you, and notice one specific thing they did: a meal, a ride, a hand on your shoulder.
Let your breath stay with that picture, and if you pray, hold them in your prayer.
